content: Approximately 10% of women of reproductive age are affected by endometriosis, a chronic and costly condition that is associated with pelvic pain and infertility. The current gold standard for diagnosing endometriosis is laparoscopy, a surgical procedure that is both expensive and carries inherent risks. At present, there are no reliable non-invasive or minimally invasive diagnostic tests available in clinical practice to accurately identify endometriosis. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of urinary biomarkers for detecting pelvic endometriosis, using surgical diagnosis as the reference standard. Additionally, the study aimed to assess whether urinary biomarkers could differentiate ovarian endometriomas from other types of ovarian masses. Urinary biomarkers were considered both as potential replacements for surgical diagnosis and as triage tools to guide decisions about whether surgery should be performed. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others, between April 20 and July 31, 2015. The search was not limited by study design, language, or publication date. The strategy included keywords, text words, and medical subject headings (MeSH) tailored to each database. Recently published but not yet indexed studies were also included. The selection criteria focused on peer-reviewed, published studies that were either randomized controlled trials or cross-sectional studies. These studies had to include prospectively collected samples from reproductive-aged women suspected of having ovarian, peritoneal, or deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE). The diagnostic accuracy of urinary biomarkers was compared to the surgical visualization of endometriotic lesions. Two independent authors collected and assessed the quality of data from each study. Diagnostic test results were classified as positive or negative based on surgical findings, and sensitivity and specificity were calculated. If multiple tests were evaluated within the same cohort, each test was treated as a separate dataset. A bivariate model was used to pool sensitivity and specificity estimates when sufficient data were available. For a urinary biomarker to replace diagnostic surgery, it needed to achieve a sensitivity of 94% and a specificity of 79%. For triage tests, the criteria were either a sensitivity of ≥95% and specificity of ≥50% (to rule out endometriosis in negative cases, known as a SnOUT test) or a sensitivity of ≥50% and specificity of ≥95% (to confirm endometriosis in positive cases, known as a SpIN test). The study included eight studies involving 646 participants, most of which were of poor methodological quality. The urinary biomarkers were evaluated either during specific phases of the menstrual cycle or without regard to cycle phase. Five studies assessed the diagnostic performance of four urinary biomarkers for endometriosis. These included enolase 1 (NNE), vitamin D binding protein (VDBP), and urinary peptide profiling, which showed some ability to distinguish women with endometriosis from those without. However, cytokeratin 19 (CK 19) did not show significant differences between the two groups. All biomarkers were evaluated in small individual studies, and the data were insufficient for meaningful statistical analysis. None of the biomarkers met the criteria for either a replacement test or a triage test. Additionally, three studies evaluated three other biomarkers that failed to differentiate women with endometriosis from those without the disease. The authors concluded that there is currently insufficient evidence to recommend any urinary biomarker for use as a replacement or triage test in clinical practice for diagnosing endometriosis. While some urinary biomarkers may have diagnostic potential, further research is needed before they can be implemented in routine clinical settings. For now, laparoscopy remains the gold standard for diagnosing endometriosis, and the use of urinary biomarkers for this purpose should be confined to research contexts.
